newsitem.title: USA: Motorola's naming Galvin praised on Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Motorola's naming Galvin praised on Wall Street.

text.p: Motorola Inc.'s decision to appoint Christopher Galvin, grandson of the company's legendary founder, as its next chief executive won praise from Wall Street on Friday.

"I think Chris Galvin is the right man for the job right now," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for Gruntal & Co. "Galvin moving up and really having full control over operations is really important. He has a lot of vision and is innovative."
Motorola said on Thursday that Galvin, 46, will take the company's reins as chief executive Jan. 1, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and father.

"I really think that Chris Galvin has been groomed for this for a long time," said Jim Buckman, co-director of the Quality Leadership Center at the Carlton School of Management at the University of Minnesota.
"There's every evidence that this is a planned succession, that they've been working for this for a long time and that he is ready," Buckman said.
Galvin, who began his career at Motorla 24 years ago in sales and product management, is currently the company's president and chief operating officer.

Motorola, struggling recently with an industry-wide slump in semiconductors and stiff competition in cellular phones, said Chairman William Weisz will step down Jan. 1 and be succeeded by Gary Tooker, 57, the current chief executive.
Weisz turns 70 in January and company rules call for directors not to seek re-election at the annual meeting after their 70th birthday.
Motorola was founded by Paul Galvin in 1928, originally to manufacture car radios, and has been credited with inventing two-way radio communication, used initially in police cars, during his tenure.
Management of the company eventually was passed down to Bob Galvin, Paul Galvin's son and Chris Galvin's father.

"Paul Galvin was pretty convinced that there was a right way, a values-driven way, a visionary way of doing business, and that's what he successfully passed on to his son Bob, who continued it," Buckman said.
Bob Galvin took the company into its next generation, the cellular telephone business, and implemented a "total quality" standard, a corporate culture the company continues to embrace.
"Bob Galvin is still a meaningful factor in the company as an advisor and a futurist," Robert Gutenstein, director of research at Kalb, Voorhis & Co, an investment bank, said.
"Motorola is a company whose underlying premise is managing continuing renewal," Chris Galvin said in an interview following announcement of the management change.

Galvin will be replaced as chief operating officer and president by Robert Growney, who currently serves as executive vice president and general manager of the Messaging, Information and Media Sector.

"He (Growney) has headed a division which has grown from nothing to very important," Albert Lin, an analyst for Cowen & Co, said. The sector, which includes paging products, accounts for about 12 percent of Motorola's total revenues.
"Even though he has been quiet and soft-spoken, the bottom line is (that) under his tenure, he has put Motorola solidly on the map as the dominant player in paging," Lin said.
Analysts said Chris Galvin's passion is the realization of the company's Iridium global telecommunications project and other satellite-based communications networks.
Motorola stock fell 87.5 cents to $53.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
